question: A company uses a third-party SaaS monitoring tool that needs to receive data from resources in a private VPC subnet with no internet access. The SaaS vendor has published their service as an AWS PrivateLink-enabled endpoint service. The security team requires that traffic to the SaaS provider never traverses the public internet and remains entirely within the AWS network.

options.A: Peer the company's VPC directly with the SaaS vendor's VPC using VPC Peering.
options.B: Configure a NAT Gateway with a route to an internet gateway, then allow-list the vendor's public IP ranges in the security group.
options.C: Set up a Site-to-Site VPN connection to the SaaS vendor's data center.
options.D: Create an interface VPC endpoint in the private subnet pointing to the vendor's PrivateLink service, and route traffic to the endpoint's private IP address.

explanation: A company uses a third-party SaaS monitoring tool that needs to receive data from resources in a private VPC subnet with no internet access. The SaaS vendor has published their service as an AWS PrivateLink-enabled endpoint service. The security team requires that traffic to the SaaS provider never traverses the public internet and remains entirely within the AWS network. A. Peer the company's VPC directly with the SaaS vendor's VPC using VPC Peering. B. Configure a NAT Gateway with a route to an internet gateway, then allow-list the vendor's public IP ranges in the security group. C. Set up a Site-to-Site VPN connection to the SaaS vendor's data center. D. ✓ Create an interface VPC endpoint in the private subnet pointing to the vendor's PrivateLink service, and route traffic to the endpoint's private IP address. An interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink creates an ENI with a private IP in the subnet that privately connects to the vendor's published endpoint service, ensuring traffic stays entirely on the AWS network and never traverses the public internet, matching exactly what the vendor offers and what security requires. B is wrong because routing through a NAT Gateway and internet gateway sends traffic over the public internet path, violating the requirement, regardless of IP allow-listing. C is impractical and wrong: Site-to-Site VPN connects to an on-premises network via a customer gateway, not to a SaaS vendor's AWS-hosted service, and the vendor has not offered this as a connectivity option. A is wrong because VPC Peering requires full network-level peering between both parties and non-overlapping CIDR coordination; PrivateLink exists specifically to avoid this by exposing a single service endpoint rather than the entire network, which is exactly why the vendor published PrivateLink instead of offering peering. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 50

whyOthersAreWrong.B: Configure a NAT Gateway with a route to an internet gateway, then allow-list the vendor's public IP ranges in the security group.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Option C (Set up a Site-to-Site VPN connection to the SaaS vendor's data center.) is suboptimal because it fails to satisfy the stated operational, architectural, or cost constraints.

question: A security team wants to require that IAM users can only terminate EC2 instances or delete S3 buckets if they have authenticated with multi-factor authentication in their current session, while still allowing all other read-only actions without MFA.

options.A: Attach an IAM policy that denies the specific destructive actions, such as ec2:TerminateInstances and s3:DeleteBucket, unless the condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true.
options.B: Enable MFA as a mandatory requirement for all IAM sign-ins account-wide via the account settings.
options.C: Require MFA only at the AWS Organizations management account level, which cascades the requirement to all IAM users in member accounts.
options.D: Use IAM Access Analyzer to automatically block any API call made without an active MFA device registered.

explanation: A security team wants to require that IAM users can only terminate EC2 instances or delete S3 buckets if they have authenticated with multi-factor authentication in their current session, while still allowing all other read-only actions without MFA. A. ✓ Attach an IAM policy that denies the specific destructive actions, such as ec2:TerminateInstances and s3:DeleteBucket, unless the condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true. B. Enable MFA as a mandatory requirement for all IAM sign-ins account-wide via the account settings. C. Require MFA only at the AWS Organizations management account level, which cascades the requirement to all IAM users in member accounts. D. Use IAM Access Analyzer to automatically block any API call made without an active MFA device registered. An explicit Deny statement scoped to the specific destructive actions, with a condition on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, is the standard IAM pattern to enforce step-up MFA for sensitive operations while leaving other actions unaffected, since an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow. B is wrong because there is no native account-wide toggle that forces MFA for all IAM sign-ins, and even if there were, it would not achieve the granular "only for destructive actions" requirement. C is wrong because the management account's MFA settings do not cascade to or enforce anything on IAM users in member accounts; each account's IAM configuration is independent unless an SCP or IAM policy specifically enforces it. D is wrong because IAM Access Analyzer is a policy analysis and unused-access review tool for identifying overly permissive or externally exposed access; it does not enforce runtime MFA conditions on API calls. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 51

whyOthersAreWrong.B: Enable MFA as a mandatory requirement for all IAM sign-ins account-wide via the account settings.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Require MFA only at the AWS Organizations management account level, which cascades the requirement to all IAM users in member accounts.

options.A: Install a third-party antivirus agent on every EC2 instance and configure it to run a full disk scan whenever CPU utilization spikes.
options.B: Enable GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2, which automatically triggers agentless scanning of EBS snapshot data when a relevant GuardDuty finding occurs, without needing an agent on the running instance.
options.C: Use Amazon Inspector network reachability scans, which automatically scan EBS volumes for malware signatures.

question: A central networking account owns a Transit Gateway that must be used by 15 spoke accounts in the same AWS Organization to connect their VPCs together, without each spoke account's administrators being able to modify the Transit Gateway's route tables or attachments belonging to other spokes.

options.A: Manually recreate a copy of the Transit Gateway in each spoke account and peer them all together.
options.B: Grant each spoke account's administrators full IAM access to the Transit Gateway resource in the central account so they can create their own attachments and manage routing directly.
options.C: Share the Transit Gateway with the spoke accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager, allowing each spoke account to create its own VPC attachment, while the central account retains control over route table associations and propagations that cannot be altered by spoke administrators.
options.D: Use VPC Peering between the central account's VPC and each of the 15 spoke VPCs instead of a Transit Gateway.

explanation: A central networking account owns a Transit Gateway that must be used by 15 spoke accounts in the same AWS Organization to connect their VPCs together, without each spoke account's administrators being able to modify the Transit Gateway's route tables or attachments belonging to other spokes. Grant each spoke account's administrators full IAM access to the Transit Gateway resource in the central account so they can create their own attachments and manage routing directly. C. ✓ Share the Transit Gateway with the spoke accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager, allowing each spoke account to create its own VPC attachment, while the central account retains control over route table associations and propagations that cannot be altered by spoke administrators. D. Use VPC Peering between the central account's VPC and each of the 15 spoke VPCs instead of a Transit Gateway. D scales poorly: full-mesh VPC Peering among 15-plus VPCs grows in complexity with every pair, has no transitive routing, and loses the centralized route management a Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke design provides. question: A company discovers that a developer accidentally set an S3 bucket's ACL to public-read, exposing sensitive files. The security team wants to prevent this specific type of accidental exposure from ever happening again across all current and future buckets in the account, with a single account-level setting.

options.A: Manually review every bucket's ACL weekly and revert any public settings found.
options.B: Set up a Service Control Policy that denies the s3:PutBucketAcl action across the Organization.
options.C: Delete all bucket ACLs and rely solely on IAM policies to control access going forward.
options.D: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level, which overrides any bucket ACL or bucket policy that would otherwise grant public access, for all current and future buckets. Design Resilient Architectures

Delete all bucket ACLs and rely solely on IAM policies to control access going forward. D. ✓ Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level, which overrides any bucket ACL or bucket policy that would otherwise grant public access, for all current and future buckets. S3 Block Public Access at the account level is a single control-plane setting that overrides or blocks any public ACLs or bucket policies for every bucket in the account, both existing and newly created, exactly matching the "single account-level setting, current and future buckets" requirement, and is AWS's recommended baseline for preventing accidental public exposure. question: A company runs a mission-critical Aurora MySQL database in us-east-1 and must be able to recover in eu-west-1 within an RTO of under 1 minute and an RPO of under 1 second in the event of a full regional outage, with the ability to redirect application writes to the secondary region during failover.

options.A: Configure Aurora Global Database with us-east-1 as the primary and eu-west-1 as a secondary region, which uses dedicated, purpose-built storage-layer replication achieving typical replication lag under 1 second, and use managed failover to promote the secondary for writes.
options.B: Configure a standard Aurora MySQL cross-region read replica in eu-west-1 using standard MySQL binlog replication, and manually promote it if us-east-1 fails.
options.C: Set up an Aurora Multi-AZ cluster within us-east-1 only, since Multi-AZ alone provides cross-region resilience.
options.D: Use AWS Database Migration Service as an ongoing, full-time replication mechanism from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 for disaster recovery. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 11

A. ✓ Configure Aurora Global Database with us-east-1 as the primary and eu-west-1 as a secondary region, which uses dedicated, purpose-built storage-layer replication achieving typical replication lag under 1 second, and use managed failover to promote the secondary for writes. B. Configure a standard Aurora MySQL cross-region read replica in eu-west-1 using standard MySQL binlog replication, and manually promote it if us-east-1 fails. C. Set up an Aurora Multi-AZ cluster within us-east-1 only, since Multi-AZ alone provides cross-region resilience. D. Use AWS Database Migration Service as an ongoing, full-time replication mechanism from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 for disaster recovery. Aurora Global Database is purpose-built for this exact requirement: it uses dedicated replication infrastructure at the storage layer, separate from user-space MySQL binlog replication, achieving typically sub-1-second cross-region replication lag, and supports managed failover that can promote a secondary region to accept writes within about a minute. B is wrong because standard binlog-based cross-region read replicas have materially higher and more variable replication lag, and manual promotion adds further delay, failing to reliably meet the stated targets. C is wrong because Multi-AZ provides resilience against an Availability Zone failure within a single Region, not protection against a full Regional outage. D is wrong because DMS is designed for migration, not as the purpose-built, lowest-latency mechanism for Aurora-to-Aurora cross-region disaster recovery, and typically has higher replication lag and operational complexity for this specific use case. question: A team configured an RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ instance for high availability. During a recent AZ outage, the application experienced roughly 60 to 90 seconds of downtime before recovering automatically. The team wants to understand why a read replica was not used and whether promoting a read replica would have been faster.

options.A: A read replica promotion would have been faster and should be used instead of Multi-AZ, since promotion completes in single-digit seconds.
options.B: Multi-AZ deployments already provide the fastest automatic failover AWS offers for standard RDS engines, typically 60 to 120 seconds via a DNS endpoint flip to the synchronously replicated standby; a read replica promotion is a separate, manual or scripted mechanism using asynchronous replication that typically takes longer once reconnection is accounted for.
options.C: The observed downtime indicates a misconfiguration; Multi-AZ failover should always complete in under 5 seconds and something was set up incorrectly.
options.D: Read replicas and Multi-AZ standbys are the same underlying feature in RDS, just named differently, so there would be no difference in failover time. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 12

explanation: A team configured an RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ instance for high availability. During a recent AZ outage, the application experienced roughly 60 to 90 seconds of downtime before recovering automatically. The team wants to understand why a read replica was not used and whether promoting a read replica would have been faster. A. A read replica promotion would have been faster and should be used instead of Multi-AZ, since promotion completes in single-digit seconds. B. ✓ Multi-AZ deployments already provide the fastest automatic failover AWS offers for standard RDS engines, typically 60 to 120 seconds via a DNS endpoint flip to the synchronously replicated standby; a read replica promotion is a separate, manual or scripted mechanism using asynchronous replication that typically takes longer once reconnection is accounted for. C. The observed downtime indicates a misconfiguration; Multi-AZ failover should always complete in under 5 seconds and something was set up incorrectly. D. Read replicas and Multi-AZ standbys are the same underlying feature in RDS, just named differently, so there would be no difference in failover time. Standard RDS Multi-AZ, for engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL, uses synchronous block-level replication to a standby in a different AZ, and automatic failover typically completes within 60 to 120 seconds as AWS flips the DNS endpoint to the standby -- matching the observed behavior and representing correctly configured, expected operation. A is wrong because read replicas use asynchronous replication and promotion is not an automatic failover mechanism; it requires manual or scripted intervention and is generally not faster once reconnection overhead is included. C is wrong because 60 to 120 seconds is the normal, documented range for standard RDS Multi-AZ failover, not evidence of misconfiguration; sub-5-second failover requires Aurora's different Multi-AZ cluster architecture. D is factually incorrect: Multi-AZ standby instances are not independently accessible and use synchronous replication for HA, while read replicas use asynchronous replication and are separately queryable -- they are distinct features with different replication models. question: A containerized web application running as an ECS Fargate service must remain available even if an entire Availability Zone fails, automatically replacing unhealthy tasks, and distributing incoming traffic only to healthy tasks. Design the resilient architecture.

options.A: Run all Fargate tasks in a single AZ behind an Application Load Balancer to simplify networking, and rely on ECS to relaunch tasks quickly if the AZ fails.
options.B: Use a single large EC2 instance to host all containers instead of Fargate, since the EC2 launch type is inherently more resilient than Fargate.
options.C: Configure the ECS service with its desired task count spread across subnets in at least two, ideally three, Availability Zones, place the service behind an Application Load Balancer with target group health checks, and let the ECS service scheduler automatically replace unhealthy or failed tasks to maintain the desired count.
options.D: Configure the Fargate tasks with a single Elastic IP shared across all tasks for simplicity.

explanation: A containerized web application running as an ECS Fargate service must remain available even if an entire Availability Zone fails, automatically replacing unhealthy tasks, and distributing incoming traffic only to healthy tasks. Design the resilient architecture. A. Run all Fargate tasks in a single AZ behind an Application Load Balancer to simplify networking, and rely on ECS to relaunch tasks quickly if the AZ fails. B. Use a single large EC2 instance to host all containers instead of Fargate, since the EC2 launch type is inherently more resilient than Fargate. C. ✓ Configure the ECS service with its desired task count spread across subnets in at least two, ideally three, Availability Zones, place the service behind an Application Load Balancer with target group health checks, and let the ECS service scheduler automatically replace unhealthy or failed tasks to maintain the desired count. D. Configure the Fargate tasks with a single Elastic IP shared across all tasks for simplicity. The correct resilient design spreads the service's tasks across multiple AZs via subnets in the network configuration, fronts them with an ALB whose target group health checks deregister and replace unhealthy targets, and relies on the ECS service scheduler to continuously reconcile actual versus desired task count, automatically launching replacements when tasks fail or an AZ becomes unavailable. A is wrong because placing all tasks in a single AZ means an AZ failure takes down the entire service; relaunching quickly does not help if that AZ itself is unavailable for new task placement. B is wrong because the EC2-versus-Fargate launch type choice governs the compute management model, not inherent resilience; either launch type can be made resilient or not depending on how tasks are distributed across AZs. D is wrong and does not reflect how Fargate networking works for a load-balanced service: tasks receive their own ENIs and private IPs, and traffic is distributed via the ALB and target groups, not a single shared Elastic IP. question: (Select TWO) A company stores critical business documents in an S3 bucket in us-east-1 and needs the data to be resilient to a full regional failure, automatically and continuously replicated to a bucket in us-west-2, while also being protected against accidental object deletion or overwrite in the source region. Which TWO configurations are required?

options.A: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication from the us-east-1 bucket to a bucket in us-west-2.
options.B: Enable Versioning on both the source and destination buckets, since Cross-Region Replication requires versioning on both buckets, and versioning also protects against accidental overwrites and deletes by preserving prior object versions.
options.C: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the source bucket, which is required for any cross-region data transfer to succeed.
options.D: Configure Same-Region Replication first, since it is a prerequisite that must be enabled before Cross-Region Replication can be configured.
options.E: Manually run an AWS CLI sync script on a nightly cron job to copy new objects between the buckets.

explanation: (Select TWO) A company stores critical business documents in an S3 bucket in us-east-1 and needs the data to be resilient to a full regional failure, automatically and continuously replicated to a bucket in us-west-2, while also being protected against accidental object deletion or overwrite in the source region. Which TWO configurations are required? A. ✓ Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication from the us-east-1 bucket to a bucket in us-west-2. B. ✓ Enable Versioning on both the source and destination buckets, since Cross-Region Replication requires versioning on both buckets, and versioning also protects against accidental overwrites and deletes by preserving prior object versions. C. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the source bucket, which is required for any cross-region data transfer to succeed. D. Configure Same-Region Replication first, since it is a prerequisite that must be enabled before Cross-Region Replication can be configured. E. Manually run an AWS CLI sync script on a nightly cron job to copy new objects between the buckets. Cross-Region Replication (A) is the native S3 feature for continuous, automatic, asynchronous replication of objects to a bucket in another region for exactly this DR use case; CRR has a hard requirement that versioning be enabled on both source and destination buckets (B), and versioning independently protects against accidental deletes or overwrites by retaining previous object versions. C is wrong because Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads into S3 over long distances via CloudFront edge locations and is unrelated to, and not required for, CRR. D is wrong because Same-Region Replication and Cross-Region Replication are independent, alternative configurations; SRR is not a prerequisite for CRR. E is wrong because a manual scheduled sync script is not automatic and continuous as required, only runs when triggered, leaving gaps, and requires ongoing operational maintenance compared to the native, event-driven CRR feature. question: A gaming company needs a player-profile database that supports low-latency reads and writes from users in both North America and Europe simultaneously, with each region's writes automatically propagated to the other region, and the ability to continue operating, in a degraded eventually-consistent manner, if one region becomes unavailable.

options.A: DynamoDB Global Tables configured across us-east-1 and eu-west-1, providing multi-active replication where applications in each region read and write to their local table replica, with changes automatically propagated cross-region.
options.B: A single DynamoDB table in us-east-1 with a cross-region read replica in eu-west-1 for read scaling, while all writes go to us-east-1.
options.C: Two entirely separate DynamoDB tables, one per region, with a nightly AWS Glue ETL job synchronizing the data between them.
options.D: Amazon Aurora MySQL Global Database instead, since DynamoDB does not support any multi-region replication features. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 14

C is wrong because a nightly batch ETL sync is not near-real-time replication and would leave both tables significantly out of sync for up to 24 hours. question: A company runs its primary website on an ALB in us-east-1 and maintains a static "we're down" S3-hosted backup site in us-west-2. They want DNS to automatically route users to the backup site only when the primary ALB fails health checks, and automatically route back to the primary once it recovers.

options.A: Configure a Route 53 weighted routing policy with 90 percent of traffic to the primary and 10 percent to the backup at all times.
options.B: Configure a Route 53 failover routing policy with a primary record pointing to the ALB, associated with a Route 53 health check monitoring the ALB, and a secondary record pointing to the S3 static site; Route 53 automatically shifts DNS answers to the secondary when the primary health check fails, and back once it recovers.
options.C: Configure a Route 53 latency-based routing policy between the ALB and the S3 static website endpoint.
options.D: Manually update the DNS record to point to the backup site whenever the operations team notices the primary is down.

explanation: A company runs its primary website on an ALB in us-east-1 and maintains a static "we're down" S3-hosted backup site in us-west-2. They want DNS to automatically route users to the backup site only when the primary ALB fails health checks, and automatically route back to the primary once it recovers. A. Configure a Route 53 weighted routing policy with 90 percent of traffic to the primary and 10 percent to the backup at all times. B. ✓ Configure a Route 53 failover routing policy with a primary record pointing to the ALB, associated with a Route 53 health check monitoring the ALB, and a secondary record pointing to the S3 static site; Route 53 automatically shifts DNS answers to the secondary when the primary health check fails, and back once it recovers. C. Configure a Route 53 latency-based routing policy between the ALB and the S3 static website endpoint. D. Manually update the DNS record to point to the backup site whenever the operations team notices the primary is down. Route 53's failover routing policy is specifically designed for active-passive DR scenarios: it uses an associated health check on the primary record and automatically returns the secondary record's answer when the health check indicates failure, then automatically reverts once the primary's health check passes again, with no manual intervention. A is wrong because weighted routing splits traffic proportionally at all times regardless of health, sending users to the backup even when the primary is healthy, and does not provide full automatic failover on actual failure. C is wrong because latency-based routing sends users to whichever endpoint has the lowest latency, not based on health state, and does not provide the described automatic failover-on-failure behavior. D is wrong because it is a manual process with human latency and error risk, directly contradicting the "automatically" requirement. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 62

whyOthersAreWrong.D: Manually update the DNS record to point to the backup site whenever the operations team notices the primary is down. Route 53's failover routing policy is specifically designed for activ.

question: An order-processing Lambda function occasionally fails due to transient downstream service errors, and when it fails repeatedly for a specific message, that message should not be lost or block processing of other orders -- it should be captured for later investigation without endless retries. Design the resilient decoupled architecture.

options.A: Have the order API call the processing Lambda function synchronously and directly, with the client responsible for retrying failed requests.
options.B: Use an SQS FIFO queue with a maxReceiveCount of 1, since FIFO queues automatically discard failed messages after a single attempt.
options.C: Place a standard SQS queue between the order API and the processing Lambda, with Lambda polling the queue as an event source, configure a redrive policy with a maxReceiveCount, and set up a dead-letter queue to capture messages that fail processing repeatedly, isolating problem messages without blocking the main queue.
options.D: Configure the Lambda function with a longer timeout so that it never fails. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 15

explanation: An order-processing Lambda function occasionally fails due to transient downstream service errors, and when it fails repeatedly for a specific message, that message should not be lost or block processing of other orders -- it should be captured for later investigation without endless retries. Design the resilient decoupled architecture. A. Have the order API call the processing Lambda function synchronously and directly, with the client responsible for retrying failed requests. B. Use an SQS FIFO queue with a maxReceiveCount of 1, since FIFO queues automatically discard failed messages after a single attempt. C. ✓ Place a standard SQS queue between the order API and the processing Lambda, with Lambda polling the queue as an event source, configure a redrive policy with a maxReceiveCount, and set up a dead-letter queue to capture messages that fail processing repeatedly, isolating problem messages without blocking the main queue. D. Configure the Lambda function with a longer timeout so that it never fails. This is the standard asynchronous decoupling pattern: SQS buffers orders between producer and consumer, Lambda consumes via the SQS event source mapping, and a redrive policy combined with a dead-letter queue ensures messages that repeatedly fail are automatically moved out of the main queue for later investigation, preventing a poison-pill message from blocking or endlessly cycling through processing while preserving it rather than losing it. A is wrong because synchronous direct invocation tightly couples the API and processing function, provides no buffering, and pushes retry responsibility to the client with no resilience against transient failures. B is wrong because FIFO queues do not automatically discard failed messages; a dead-letter queue must still be explicitly configured to capture them, or the message would simply keep cycling rather than being safely isolated. D is wrong because extending the timeout does not fix the root cause of transient downstream errors and provides no mechanism to capture messages that genuinely fail. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 63

question: An Auto Scaling Group launches new EC2 instances that require several minutes of custom software installation and configuration via a startup script before they can safely begin receiving production traffic from the attached ALB. Currently, the ALB starts sending traffic to new instances before they have finished initializing, causing errors. Fix this.

options.A: Increase the ALB's health check interval to 5 minutes so it checks less frequently.
options.B: Set the ASG's health check grace period to 0 seconds so instances are checked immediately.
options.C: Remove the ALB and use DNS round-robin directly to instance IP addresses instead.
options.D: Configure an Auto Scaling lifecycle hook on instance launch that keeps the instance in a wait state until the initialization script completes and signals completion, combined with the ALB target group health check, so the instance only enters service after initialization finishes and health checks pass.

Increase the ALB's health check interval to 5 minutes so it checks less frequently. B. Set the ASG's health check grace period to 0 seconds so instances are checked immediately. C. Remove the ALB and use DNS round-robin directly to instance IP addresses instead. question: A company's on-premises legacy application, with an RPO of 1 hour and an RTO of 4 hours acceptable to the business, needs a disaster recovery plan in AWS. The business wants the lowest-cost DR strategy that still meets these RPO and RTO targets, avoiding the cost of running duplicate full-scale infrastructure continuously in AWS.

options.A: Pilot light: continuously replicate data to AWS, such as via ongoing database replication or AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, keep only the minimal core infrastructure like the database always running, and keep the rest of the environment pre-configured but stopped, scaling it up only during an actual failover.
options.B: Multi-site active/active: run a full production-scale duplicate environment continuously in AWS, synchronized in real time with on-premises, for the fastest possible failover with near-zero RTO and RPO.
options.C: Backup and restore: back up data to AWS and, in a disaster, provision and restore all infrastructure from scratch; this is the lowest raw cost, but RTO is typically measured in many hours to days, which may not reliably meet a 4-hour RTO for a full application stack.
options.D: Rely solely on tape backups shipped to a third-party offsite storage facility, with no AWS DR infrastructure at all. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 16

question: A global company has VPCs in three AWS Regions -- us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1 -- each containing multiple VPCs that need to communicate with each other, plus connectivity to on-premises data centers in each geographic area, with centralized, simplified route management rather than a complex full mesh.

options.A: Create VPC Peering connections between every pair of VPCs across all three regions, resulting in a full mesh.
options.B: Deploy a Transit Gateway in each region, since a single Transit Gateway is regional, connect the in-region VPCs and on-premises Direct Connect or VPN links to each regional Transit Gateway, and use Transit Gateway peering to interconnect the three regional Transit Gateways for inter-region traffic.
options.C: Use a single Transit Gateway created in us-east-1 and attach the VPCs from eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1 directly to it, since Transit Gateway is a global service.
options.D: Use AWS Global Accelerator to connect the VPCs across the three regions instead of Transit Gateway.

Use AWS Global Accelerator to connect the VPCs across the three regions instead of Transit Gateway. D is wrong because Global Accelerator improves availability and performance for internet-facing endpoints; it is not a VPC-to-VPC private networking or routing solution. question: An order fulfillment workflow involves calling multiple services in sequence -- payment, inventory reservation, and shipping label creation -- with different retry and backoff needs per step, and if a step fails permanently after retries, previously completed steps such as payment must be automatically compensated, for example refunded, rather than left in an inconsistent state.

options.A: Chain the services together using direct synchronous Lambda-to-Lambda invocations, with each Lambda responsible for calling the next.
options.B: Use Amazon SQS alone, with each service polling the same queue and manually implementing its own compensation logic in application code with no central orchestration.
options.C: Use AWS Step Functions with a state machine defining each step, per-step Retry and Catch configurations for error handling and backoff, and error-handling states that trigger compensating actions when a downstream step fails permanently.
options.D: Use EventBridge Scheduler to invoke each of the three services independently every minute, checking a database flag to determine which step to run next. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 17

A. Chain the services together using direct synchronous Lambda-to-Lambda invocations, with each Lambda responsible for calling the next. B. Use Amazon SQS alone, with each service polling the same queue and manually implementing its own compensation logic in application code with no central orchestration. C. ✓ Use AWS Step Functions with a state machine defining each step, per-step Retry and Catch configurations for error handling and backoff, and error-handling states that trigger compensating actions when a downstream step fails permanently. D. Use EventBridge Scheduler to invoke each of the three services independently every minute, checking a database flag to determine which step to run next. Step Functions is purpose-built for this kind of multi-step, stateful workflow orchestration, providing native per-state Retry and Catch fields, allowing an explicit compensating-transaction, or Saga, pattern where a permanent downstream failure routes execution to states that undo prior successful steps, with built-in execution history for auditing. B is wrong because a shared queue with fully decentralized compensation logic and no central orchestrator makes it very difficult to reliably coordinate multi-step compensating transactions. D is wrong and inefficient, introducing unnecessary per-step latency and reinventing workflow state management poorly compared to Step Functions. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 67

question: A media company replicates its content bucket across three regions using S3 Cross-Region Replication for redundancy, but currently application code must be manually updated with region-specific bucket endpoints, and failover to another region's bucket during an outage requires a code deployment. They want a single, static endpoint that automatically routes S3 requests to the lowest-latency healthy replica, without app changes during failover.

options.A: Manually maintain a config file listing all three bucket endpoints and add custom failover logic in every application.
options.B: Use Route 53 latency-based routing directly pointed at each bucket's regional endpoint, with three separate DNS records.
options.C: Put a Network Load Balancer in front of the three regional S3 bucket endpoints.
options.D: Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point spanning the three replicated buckets; applications use the single Multi-Region Access Point global endpoint, and S3 automatically routes requests to the lowest-latency bucket, with automatic failover routing away from a bucket experiencing an outage.

explanation: A media company replicates its content bucket across three regions using S3 Cross-Region Replication for redundancy, but currently application code must be manually updated with region-specific bucket endpoints, and failover to another region's bucket during an outage requires a code deployment. They want a single, static endpoint that automatically routes S3 requests to the lowest-latency healthy replica, without app changes during failover. A. Manually maintain a config file listing all three bucket endpoints and add custom failover logic in every application. B. Use Route 53 latency-based routing directly pointed at each bucket's regional endpoint, with three separate DNS records. C. Put a Network Load Balancer in front of the three regional S3 bucket endpoints. D. ✓ Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point spanning the three replicated buckets; applications use the single Multi-Region Access Point global endpoint, and S3 automatically routes requests to the lowest-latency bucket, with automatic failover routing away from a bucket experiencing an outage. S3 Multi-Region Access Points are designed for exactly this use case: they provide a single global endpoint backed by the underlying replicated buckets, automatically routing each request to the lowest-latency healthy bucket and failing over automatically if a Region becomes unavailable, entirely transparent to the application. A is exactly the manual, brittle, code-change-requiring approach the company wants to eliminate. C is wrong because a Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 for TCP or UDP traffic to registered targets; it is not designed to, and cannot, front S3 bucket endpoints as a routing mechanism. B is a plausible but inferior alternative, requiring management of multiple DNS records and health checks manually, and does not natively understand S3 replication status the way the purpose-built Multi-Region Access Point feature does. question: (Select TWO) A company must retain encrypted backups of its RDS databases and EBS volumes for 7 years for regulatory compliance, with backups automatically and continuously copied to a second AWS Region shortly after creation, and wants a single, centrally managed policy across all its accounts and resource types rather than configuring each service's native backup feature separately. options.A: Use AWS Backup with a backup plan defining a schedule, a 7-year retention lifecycle rule, and a cross-Region copy action to automatically copy each recovery point to a backup vault in a second Region shortly after creation.
